title: Represent a Fraction Greater Than One on a Number Line
goal: I can count fractional units beyond one and compare a fraction with one.
catchAll: Keep the denominator fixed as you pass one. A numerator larger than the denominator means more than one whole.

teacher.def: The denominator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are in the whole. It is the bottom part of the fraction
A unit fraction is ONE part of a whole. It always has a numerator of one.
The numerator of a fraction tells how many equal parts are being described. It is the top part of the fraction.
A fraction is a number used when a whole is split into equal parts.

glossary.whole: the one shape, unit length, complete piece or entire set named in the question
glossary.partition: divide a whole into equal parts
glossary.interval: the distance between neighboring marks on a number line

screens.title: Name the whole
text: Keep the same interval size across all whole units.

screens.title: Connect the parts
text: Count fractional intervals continuously beyond one.
Keep the denominator fixed as you pass one. A numerator larger than the denominator means more than one whole.

screens.title: Check the reasoning
text: Compare the numerator with the denominator to decide whether the value is below, at or above one.

item.prompt: How can you tell from the numerator and denominator that a fraction is greater than one? Write a complete sentence.
item.example: When the numerator is greater than the denominator, the counted parts include a whole and additional equal parts, so the value is greater than one.
hints: Describe what the whole is and how its parts are counted.
show: Compare your reasoning with a grown-up or the model response.
When the numerator is greater than the denominator, the counted parts include a whole and additional equal parts, so the value is greater than one.

examples.title: Identify the whole and what is counted

steps.say: For a wall hanging, a plan uses 1/2 of a unit. Is that less than, equal to, or greater than one whole unit?
Identify one whole unit, then count equal intervals from zero.
Counting 1 unit part gives fewer than the 2 parts in one whole, so 1/2 is less than one.
